sections.b: Ephesians 4:8-10 reads Psalm 68:18 as Christ's ascent: he went up on high, led captives, and gave gifts. The quoting of a Psalm about God's march to Zion as a word about Christ is the passage's main step. The gifts are given to every member (4:7), and the verb "fill" (4:10) ties the ascent to the whole creation, as in 1:23. The verses also raise the question of a prior descent (4:9), which the churches have read as the incarnation, the grave, or a descent to the dead.
sections.refs: Ephesians 4:8; Ephesians 4:10; Psalm 68:18; Ephesians 1:20; Acts 1:9; Hebrews 4:14

sections.h: The Spirit's unity, grief and fullness (Ephesians 4-6)
sections.b: Four things are said of the Spirit in these chapters. The Spirit makes the church one (4:3-4). The Spirit can be grieved by lies, anger and abuse, and in him believers were sealed for the day of redemption (4:30; compare Isaiah 63:10). Believers are told to be filled with the Spirit instead of wine (5:18). And prayer is made "in the Spirit" (6:18), with the "sword of the Spirit" (6:17). The grief language shows that the Spirit is personal, not just a power.
sections.refs: Ephesians 4:3; Ephesians 4:30; Ephesians 5:18; Ephesians 6:17; Ephesians 6:18; Isaiah 63:10

sections.h: "One baptism" and the washing of water (Ephesians 4:5; 5:26)
sections.b: Ephesians names one baptism among the seven "ones" that bind the church (4:5) and speaks of the church being cleansed "by the washing of water, with the spoken word" (5:26). Neither verse describes the rite or says who may receive it, and so each church has read them with its own doctrine of baptism. The call in 5:14 to "wake up" and rise from the dead is thought by many scholars to come from a baptismal hymn.

Ephesians gives marriage its longest treatment in the New Testament letters. The wife is told to submit as to the Lord, the husband to love as Christ loved the church and gave himself, and both are bound together by Genesis 2:24's "one flesh." Paul calls the union a "mystery" that speaks of Christ and the church (5:32). The Catholic and Orthodox churches count marriage a sacrament partly on that word; Protestant churches usually do not. The passage is also the center of the debate between complementarian and egalitarian readings of the home.

Ephesians addresses slaves as members of the church and tells them to serve their human masters as service to Christ, and tells masters to treat them in the same way and give up threats, since both have the same Lord, who shows no favoritism. The passage neither calls for the end of slavery nor justifies it as God's design, and it has been used both ways in history. The Philemon letter and Galatians 3:28 are the places it is usually read beside.

sections.h: Submission in Ephesians 5 and the debate over roles (Ephesians 5:21-33)
sections.b: Ephesians 5:21-33 is not about church office, but it is the household text that both sides of the debate over women's roles read beside 1 Corinthians 11 and 14 and 1 Timothy 2. Complementarians take the husband's headship (5:23) as a model for male leadership in home and church. Egalitarians take 5:21's mutual submission as the rule and read "head" as self-giving. The passage is addressed to wives as responsible persons, which was unusual in ancient household teaching.

In Ephesians the gifts are the people Christ gives to the church (apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers, 4:11), and grace is given to "each one of us" (4:7). The lists in Romans 12 and 1 Corinthians 12 name kinds of service; this one names those who ready the others. Miracles and tongues are not on the list. The aim is a body that grows up in love, with every part doing its work (4:16).

The apostles stand first in the list of Christ's gifts to the church (4:11), and in 2:20 and 3:5 they and the prophets are the foundation and the ones to whom the mystery was revealed. Whether the office continues is argued: Catholic and Orthodox churches see it carried on by the bishops; many Protestants think it ended with the first witnesses; Pentecostal and charismatic churches often teach that apostles and prophets are still given.

sections.h: Forgive as God forgave in Christ (Ephesians 4:26-32)
sections.b: Paul asks for forgiveness that is modeled on God's: "forgiving one another freely, just as God also forgave you in Christ" (4:32). The verb is built on the word for grace. The command comes in a list that includes anger that must not be stored overnight (4:26) and bitterness (4:31). Colossians 3:13 gives the same teaching.

Ephesians describes the life of the Gentiles as futile thinking and handing oneself over to impurity (4:17-19), and says that greed is itself idolatry (5:5; compare Colossians 3:5). This widens idolatry from statues to the desire for more. Ephesus, home of the great temple of Artemis (Acts 19:24-27), made the connection plain to its first readers.

Ephesians gives speech a section of its own: put away falsehood and speak truth because we are parts of one another (4:25, from Zechariah 8:16); let no rotten word come out of your mouth, but only what builds up (4:29); and leave out shameful speech, silly talk and sly joking (5:4). The test is whether the words give grace to those who hear.

The thief is told to work with his own hands, and the reason is to have something to share with the needy. Work is given a purpose beyond one's own living. Acts 20:34-35 and 1 Thessalonians 4:11 say something like it.

"Do not be drunk with wine, for reckless living is in that. Instead, be filled with the Spirit." The verse does not forbid wine, but it forbids being controlled by it, and it offers the Spirit as another way of being carried along. Some Christian traditions have used it to urge total abstinence; others read it as a warning against excess only.

sections.h: Psalms, hymns and songs from the Spirit (Ephesians 5:19)
sections.b: Ephesians names three kinds of song and asks that the church sing and "make music in your heart to the Lord" (5:19; compare Colossians 3:16). Churches have disagreed for centuries over whether this allows instruments or asks for voices only.

sections.h: Prayer in the Spirit for all the saints (Ephesians 6:18-20)
sections.b: The armor passage ends with prayer: every kind of prayer, at every moment, in the Spirit, with persistence, for all the saints. Paul asks for the same on his own behalf, that he may speak with freedom and courage (6:19-20), not that he may be freed from his chain.

The devil is warned against twice: do not give him room (4:27) and stand against his schemes (6:11). The "evil one" fires burning arrows (6:16). Ephesians sets the devil among the powers that Christ has put under his feet (1:20-22) and speaks of the ruler of the air (2:2). The church's task is to stand, not to attack.

"The sword of the Spirit, which is God's spoken word" (rhema) is the one weapon for attack in the armor. It has been read as Scripture, as the gospel message, or as a word the Spirit gives at the moment. Isaiah 11:4 and 49:2 lie behind the image of the mouth as a weapon.

sections.h: The new self created like God (Ephesians 4:24)
sections.b: The new self is "created in line with God, in the righteousness and holiness that truth brings." This is the language of Genesis 1:26-27, where humans are made in God's image, now applied to the renewal of those in Christ. Colossians 3:10 says it more openly.

sections.h: Taking off the old self, putting on the new (Ephesians 4:22-24)
sections.b: Ephesians turns Romans 6:6's "our old self was crucified" into a command: take off the old self and put on the new. The picture of clothing recalls baptism and Adam and Christ as the two heads of humanity. The new self is created and renewed (4:23-24), and the practical changes that follow (4:25-32) are what it looks like.

Children are told to obey their parents, and fathers are told not to stir their children to anger but to raise them in the Lord's discipline and warning. In a Roman household, where the father had great legal power, the second command limits the first. The word for "discipline" is the same as in the Septuagint of Proverbs.

sections.h: The fifth word with a promise (Ephesians 6:2-3)
sections.b: Paul quotes the commandment to honor father and mother and calls it "the first commandment that comes with a promise" (6:2). He changes the promise: "so that it will go well with you, and you will live long on the earth," and drops the words about the land that the LORD gives Israel. The church has long read the fifth word as the bridge between duties to God and to others.

In Ephesians Paul calls himself a prisoner (4:1; compare 3:1), an "ambassador in a chain" (6:20), and asks for prayer that he may speak freely. Where he was held is debated (Rome, Caesarea or Ephesus). Whether he wrote the letter himself or a follower wrote in his name is also debated, and the letter's portrait of him in prison is part of its authority either way.

Ephesians gives Christ the role of the husband and the church the role of the bride. He gave himself for her, cleansed her by the washing of water, and will present her to himself in glory, holy and without fault. The picture draws on the prophets' image of God as the husband of his people (Isaiah 54:5; Hosea 2:19).

sections.h: Ephesus in the letter: magic, wine and the powers (Ephesians 5:18; 6:12)
sections.b: Two features of Ephesus lie behind chapters 5 and 6. The cult of Dionysus linked wine and religious ecstasy in Asia Minor, which may sharpen the contrast between wine and the Spirit (5:18). And Ephesus was famous for magic (Acts 19:19), so a warning about the "rulers, authorities and world-rulers" (6:12) would not have sounded foreign to readers who feared such powers. Clinton Arnold's study of Ephesians reads the whole letter against this background.

Ephesians gives duties to wives and husbands, children and parents, slaves and masters. The list follows a pattern known from Aristotle's Politics and other writers, but changes it by addressing each person directly, by giving the husband the duty to love, and by grounding all of it in the Lord.
sections.refs: Ephesians 5:21; Ephesians 5:22; Ephesians 6:1; Ephesians 6:5; Colossians 3:18; 1 Peter 2:18

sections.b: Paul names a belt of truth, a breastplate of righteousness, shoes of readiness for the good news of peace, a shield of faith, a helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit. Isaiah 59:17 and 11:5 and Wisdom of Solomon 5:17-20 describe God wearing similar armor. Ephesians gives it to the church.
sections.refs: Ephesians 6:11; Ephesians 6:14; Ephesians 6:17; Isaiah 59:17; Isaiah 11:5; 1 Thessalonians 5:8

sections.b: Ephesians uses "head" of Christ in three ways: Christ is head over everything for the church (1:22), the head from whom the body grows (4:15-16), and the head of the church as the husband is head of the wife (5:23). Whether "head" in 5:23 means authority, source or prominence has been argued since the 1980s, and the answer shapes how the household code is read.

Ephesians 4:9 says Christ "came down into the lower parts of the earth." Three readings: the realm of the dead (Irenaeus; the later creed's "descended into hell"), the earth itself in the incarnation, or the regions lower than the earth. The Greek Old Testament has related phrases for the place of the dead but not this one: Psalm 63:9 (62:10 in the Greek) has "the lowest parts of the earth," a superlative, and in Ezekiel 32:18 the Greek has a phrase meaning the depth of the earth.

Ephesians 6:12 lists "the rulers, the authorities, the world-rulers of this darkness, the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly world." The first two terms appear in 1:21 and 3:10. The list has been read as personal evil beings, as the powers behind human institutions, or as a mythic way of speaking of evil. Christ is above them (1:20-22) and the church's weapons are not their own.

Tychicus was a believer from the province of Asia who traveled with Paul to Jerusalem with the collection (Acts 20:4). Ephesians 6:21-22 and Colossians 4:7-8 call him a beloved brother and faithful servant who will report on Paul and encourage the churches, and he is mentioned again in 2 Timothy 4:12 and Titus 3:12. He is the likely bearer of Ephesians.

sections.h: The body, its gifts and its growth (Ephesians 4:1-16)
sections.b: In Ephesians 4 the church is one body with one Spirit, one Lord, one faith and one baptism (4:4-5). Christ gives each member grace and gives the church people to ready it for service. The body grows from its head, held together by every joint, and builds itself up in love (4:15-16). The same chapter ties the church's life to the daily conduct of its members, who are "parts of one another" (4:25).
sections.refs: Ephesians 4:4; Ephesians 4:11; Ephesians 4:16; Ephesians 4:25; Romans 12:4; 1 Corinthians 12:12

sections.h: The great mystery of marriage and the mystery of the good news (Ephesians 5:32; 6:19)
sections.b: In 5:32 Paul calls the one-flesh union of Genesis 2:24 "a great mystery" that speaks of Christ and the church; the Latin Vulgate's sacramentum for the word is the root of the Catholic teaching that marriage is a sacrament, and Luther and Calvin rejected that reading. In 6:19 Paul asks for prayer that he may make known the mystery of the good news, which is the subject of chapter 3: Gentiles share in the promise.

sections.h: Ephesians 4-6: the walk, the household and the armor
sections.b: The second half of the letter turns the teaching of chapters 1 to 3 into conduct. The verb "walk" (4:1, 17; 5:2, 8, 15) marks its sections: unity and gifts (4:1-16), the old self and new (4:17-5:2), light and darkness (5:3-14), wisdom and the Spirit (5:15-21), the household (5:22-6:9) and the armor of God (6:10-20). It ends with Tychicus (6:21-22) and a blessing with no personal greetings. Large parts run parallel to Colossians 3:5-4:9, which is central to the question of authorship.
